definition: The title of an ancient Egyptian king, believed to be a living god who ruled over both the mortal and divine realms.
origin: From Egyptian per-aa, literally "great house," a term that originally named the royal palace itself rather than the ruler inside it. Only by the New Kingdom (around 1500 BC) did scribes begin using the phrase as a respectful way to refer to the king, much as "the White House" can stand in for a president. The word reached English via Hebrew par'oh and Greek pharao.

definition: A body, especially an ancient Egyptian one, preserved after death through embalming and wrapping so that it resists decay.
origin: English mummy descends from medieval Arabic mumiya, itself from Persian mum ("wax" or "bitumen"). Medieval traders believed Egyptian embalmed bodies had been coated in bitumen, both because of their blackened appearance and because ground "mumiya" was sold across Europe as a medicine. Only later did Egyptologists confirm the dark colour came from resins and natron salts, not tar.

definition: A tall, four-sided stone pillar that tapers to a pyramid-shaped point, originally carved by the ancient Egyptians to honour the sun god.
origin: Obelisk comes from Greek obeliskos, a diminutive of obelos ("spit" or "pointed pillar"), the same root that gives English the typographical dagger mark called an obelus. definition: A picture or symbol used in the ancient Egyptian writing system, in which signs represented sounds, objects, or ideas.
origin: Hieroglyph comes from Greek hieros ("sacred") + glyphein ("to carve"), coined because Greek visitors saw the script chiselled onto temple walls and tombs. The Egyptians themselves called their writing medu netjer, "the words of the god," believing Thoth had invented it. For nearly 1,400 years after Egypt's last native temples closed, no one could read the signs, until the Rosetta Stone provided the key.

definition: A name borne by several Ptolemaic queens of Egypt, now used to evoke the last and most famous, Cleopatra VII.
origin: Cleopatra is Greek, combining kleos ("glory") and pater ("father"), meaning roughly "glory of her father." Cleopatra VII (69–30 BC) was the last active ruler of the Ptolemaic dynasty, Greek-Macedonian kings who had governed Egypt since Alexander the Great's conquest, and her alliances with Julius Caesar and Mark Antony made her one of the ancient world's most consequential rulers.

definition: The ancient capital of Egypt near modern Cairo, founded around 3100 BC as a centre of royal power and worship of the god Ptah.
origin: Memphis is the Greek rendering of Egyptian Men-nefer, "enduring and beautiful," a name originally attached to the nearby pyramid of Pepi I and later applied to the whole city. Founded around 3100 BC, traditionally by the first king Menes, Memphis served as Egypt's political capital and chief cult centre of the creator god Ptah for much of its ancient history.

definition: Referring to the Rosetta Stone, an inscribed slab whose parallel Greek and Egyptian texts allowed scholars to decipher hieroglyphs.
origin: Rosetta is the Italian-derived name for Rashid, a town in the Nile Delta near where French soldiers unearthed the stone in 1799 while fortifying a fort. Carved in 196 BC, the stone repeats a single decree in hieroglyphic, demotic, and Greek script, and it was this parallel Greek text that let Jean-François Champollion finally crack the hieroglyphic code in 1822.

definition: The image of a rearing cobra worn on the crown of Egyptian pharaohs, symbolising royal authority and divine protection.
origin: Uraeus is a Latinised form of Greek, ultimately from Egyptian iaret, "the rearing one." It represented the goddess Wadjet, protector of Lower Egypt, shown as a cobra poised to strike enemies of the crown with spat venom or fire. Pharaohs wore it on the brow of their headdress as a constant, visible claim to divine protection and royal legitimacy.

definition: An Egyptian hieroglyphic symbol shaped like a cross with a looped top, representing life.
origin: Ankh is the Egyptian word for "life" and the hieroglyph written to spell it, a looped cross carried by gods in temple art as they granted breath and vitality to kings. Because of its shape and meaning, the ankh became one of Egypt's most enduring symbols, later adopted well beyond Egypt as jewellery and, among some early Christians in Egypt, blended with the cross.

definition: A large ancient cemetery, especially one with elaborate tombs and monuments, literally a "city of the dead."
origin: Necropolis combines Greek nekros ("corpse") and polis ("city"). Greek geographers such as Strabo used the word for Egypt's vast burial grounds at Thebes and elsewhere, cities of tombs, chapels, and processional roads that mirrored the streets and neighbourhoods of the living, built to house the dead for eternity.

definition: An enormous statue, especially one far larger than life size; figuratively, a person or thing of immense size or importance.
origin: Colossus comes from Greek kolossos, a word Greek writers used for the towering stone statues of Egyptian pharaohs long before it was famously applied to the bronze Colossus of Rhodes. The best-known Egyptian examples are the two seated Colossi of Memnon near Thebes, actually statues of Amenhotep III, which ancient Greek and Roman tourists visited to hear one figure's eerie "singing" at dawn.

definition: The great river of north-eastern Africa whose annual floods made possible the civilisation of ancient Egypt.
origin: Nile comes from Greek Neilos, a name of uncertain origin that may derive from an older Semitic or pre-Greek word for "river valley." The Egyptians themselves simply called it iteru, "the river," and personified its life-giving flood as the god Hapi, since the Nile's predictable summer inundation deposited the fertile silt that fed Egyptian agriculture for millennia.

definition: A wild, dog-like scavenger of Africa and Asia, associated in ancient Egypt with the god of embalming and the dead, Anubis.
origin: Jackal reached English via French and Turkish from Persian shaghal, tracing back to Sanskrit. In Egypt, jackals scavenged the desert edges where cemeteries lay, prompting the Egyptians to cast the animal as sacred rather than fight its presence: the black jackal-headed god Anubis was made patron and protector of embalming, guiding the dead safely through mummification and judgement.

definition: A large aquatic reptile with a long snout and armoured skin, revered in ancient Egypt as the sacred animal of the god Sobek.
origin: Crocodile comes from Greek krokodeilos, literally "pebble-worm," from kroke (pebble) + drilos (worm), a name the historian Herodotus explained as describing the lizards he saw basking on stony riverbanks. In Egypt the Nile crocodile was sacred to Sobek, a crocodile-headed god of fertility, military strength, and pharaonic power, worshipped with live crocodiles kept in temple pools.

definition: The act of forming a decision or verdict; in Egyptian belief, the trial in which a soul's heart was weighed to decide its fate.
origin: English judgement derives from Old French jugement, from Latin judicare, "to judge." The Egyptians pictured their own judgement of the dead as the Weighing of the Heart: Anubis placed the deceased's heart on a scale against the feather of Ma'at, goddess of truth, while the god Thoth recorded the result and the monster Ammit waited to devour any heart too heavy with wrongdoing.

definition: A fertile spot in a desert where water allows plants to grow, historically vital for travel and settlement.
origin: Oasis reached Greek and then Latin from Egyptian, likely via Demotic wahe or Coptic ouahe, meaning "dwelling place." Egypt's own desert oases, including Siwa, home to the temple of Amun that later gave chemistry the word "ammonia," served as vital stops for trade caravans and pilgrims crossing the vast surrounding desert.
